title: Gentleness toward yourself (III.9)
hookLine: the same mistake, a third time, and the voice in your head says "really? again?": conscience, or a second fault?
tomorrow: playoffs and finals in one week. can you be busy and not anxious?

lines: THE SAME MISTAKE, A THIRD TIME.
cards: The same mistake, a third time this week. And then the voice in your head: really? Again?
What is wrong with you? Is that voice your conscience doing its job, or one more thing going wrong? There's a real case each way, and both come from inside the tradition.
Francis de Sales gives the question its own chapter, right after gentleness toward others.

teach.h: THE CASE FOR A HARD VOICE.
teach.b: First, the case for the hard voice. The Church takes faults seriously. At Mass, in the prayer called the Confiteor, people confess aloud that they have sinned, through their own fault.
Sorrow for sin and penance are part of the life. The best case here is honest: a soft voice can slide into excuses, and feeling bad can show that you care. Now Francis's side.
Some people, he writes, fall into a fault, then get angry at being angry, upset at being upset. It feels like zeal.
He traces it to self-love: we're disturbed to find that we're imperfect, so the fury is partly about our pride. Then a picture.

A judge who passes sentence calmly, by reason, corrects better than one who sentences in a rage. The same holds inside us. A calm, firm correction reaches deeper than a storm of self-reproach, which mostly wears us out.
So when the heart falls, lift it up gently. Be humble before God about the fall, but don't be shocked by it.
He even suggests speaking to your own heart kindly, something like: poor heart, here we are, fallen into the very pit we meant to avoid; let's get up and leave it, and trust God's mercy.
Where the two sides meet: neither excuses the fault. It still gets named, and still gets fixed. The argument is about the tone of the voice that fixes it.

how: In confession, Catholics name their sins plainly and receive absolution and a penance; spiritual directors in Francis's tradition often counsel firm resolve without self-hatred.

o: never admitting to anyone that you were wrong
giving yourself a treat after a hard week
correcting your own faults calmly and firmly

games.q: two voices, one fault — tap the pairs.
p: corrects better than one in a rage
lift it gently, trust God's mercy

s: being gentle with yourself, for Francis, means not minding the fault
the fault still gets named and fixed; only the tone of the correction changes.
Francis says fury at our own faults can come from self-love
we're disturbed to find we're imperfect.
the harder you are on yourself, the faster you change, Francis says
he says a calm, firm correction reaches deeper than a storm of self-reproach.

games.q: your friend says beating herself up keeps her sharp, and "being gentle with yourself" is just an excuse. what's the best case for her side?
o: going easy can slide into excusing, and faults are serious.
feeling terrible is a punishment she owes.
God forgives only people who are hard on themselves.
games.why: that's the real case, and Francis agrees the fault must be faced. where he differs is the tone: a calm judge, not a rage.

practice: Write one mistake from this week in a single plain line. Under it, write the next small step to fix it, in the voice you'd use with a friend who did the same thing. If you pray, you can hand both lines to God's mercy.

wordCard.voice: Gentleness toward yourself. Correcting your own faults the way a calm judge would: firmly, without fury.

orig.note: Latin for meekness, gentleness: the word in the Vulgate's list of the Spirit's fruits, Galatians 5:23.

carryVoice: Your line: gentle with yourself, which is not the same as easy on yourself. Rest well.
